items.title: Tolliver interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2021
items.q: Because Art Blakey’s well-said powerful in that inimitable voice of his, you know, when he would get off the drums and speak to the audience and said, “We’re here to wash away the dust of your everyday life.”

ctx.x: Well it makes me wonder, I was sort of going to ask this question wherever our interview wraps up, but I’ll try it now. Do you feel that you have sacrificed or given anything up for this music?

Absolutely not. If I had it to do all over again I’d do exactly the same. Every bit of it you know. I mean we are blessed in a way, you know, us artisans I mean and it doesn’t matter which idiom it is: jazz music, classical music, popular music, minimalist, you know. Because Art Blakey’s well-said powerful in that inimitable voice of his, you know, when he would get off the drums and speak to the audience and said, “We’re here to wash away the dust of your everyday life.” And so I carry that in mind you know. And…
When you recorded, performed and composed, did you have something in mind that you hoped your audience would glean from your work?

items.title: Charles Tolliver interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 6, 2021 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: you know Art Blakey said it best

ctx.x: Oh absolutely. Absolutely. But also Max Roach and Clifford Brown. They created a repertory that will live forever, a repertory of using the Great American Songbook, as well as their own compositions, and putting arrangements to them that will last forever. I mean the show — Broadway writers had no idea that those beautiful songs that they wrote that became a part of the American Songbook could be completely made even better you know, with chord substitutions and rhythmical arrangements and rhythmical

displacement, and you know the American Songbook, if you are not a composer you don’t need it because it’s just so much to work with there, you know, that you can make arrangements out of. But I mean Mingus, I mean with the small group Mingus and, well, Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie, that model is still king as far as I’m concerned. If you’re getting this, yes we have all this that’s going on now, with these different types of musical theatrical events. But if you’re not dealing with that model in some…
